claim: ChAT-IRES-Cre mice crossed with Ai9(RCL-tdT) reporter line express tdTomato in cholinergic neurons.
source: Transgenic mice of both sexes expressing Cre recombinase under the endogenous choline acetyltransferase promoter (ChAT-IRES-Cre; Jackson Labs 006410) (Rossi et al., 2011) were crossed with a tdTomato reporter line (Ai9(RCL-tdT); Jackson Labs 007909) to generate mice expressing tdTomato in cholinergic neurons (referred to as ChAT-Cre/tdTomato).
evidence: The manuscript describes the genetic cross and resulting tdTomato expression in cholinergic neurons.

claim: Neurons positive for tdTomato in the LSO and VNTB co-labeled with anti-ChAT antibody, confirming they are cholinergic neurons.
source: Neurons positive for tdTomato were visible in the LSO and VNTB of the SOC, and co-labeled with anti-ChAT antibody, confirming they were cholinergic neurons (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data showing co-labeling of tdTomato and ChAT antibody confirms cholinergic identity.

claim: A majority of tdTomato-positive neurons in the ipsilateral LSO and contralateral VNTB were retrogradely labeled by injecting cholera toxin subunit B (CTB) into the cochlea.
source: A majority of tdTomato-positive neurons in the ipsilateral LSO and contralateral VNTB were retrogradely labeled by injecting cholera toxin subunit B (CTB) into the cochlea, confirming that they were indeed auditory efferent neurons (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: Retrograde tracing with CTB from the cochlea labels neurons projecting to the cochlea, confirming efferent identity.

claim: Contralateral to unilateral cochlear CTB injections, 66.1% of tdTomato-positive VNTB neurons were labeled.
source: Contralateral to unilateral cochlear CTB injections, 66.1% of tdTomato-positive VNTB neurons were labeled, and in ipsilateral VNTB, 28.9% were labeled (Figure 1F).
evidence: Quantitative data from retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: In ipsilateral VNTB, 28.9% of tdTomato-positive neurons were labeled by cochlear CTB injections.
source: Contralateral to unilateral cochlear CTB injections, 66.1% of tdTomato-positive VNTB neurons were labeled, and in ipsilateral VNTB, 28.9% were labeled (Figure 1F).
evidence: Quantitative data from retrograde tracing experiments.

claim: The majority of MOC neurons had a resting membrane potential of −80.4 ± 0.8 mV.
source: We found that the majority of MOC neurons had a resting membrane potential of −80.4 ± 0.8 mV (N = 56) and were silent at rest (only 3/59 neurons were spontaneously active), consistent with the low frequency of spontaneous activity observed in vivo (Fex, 1962; Cody and Johnstone, 1982; Robertson, 1984; Robertson and Gummer, 1985).
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings.

claim: Only 3 out of 59 MOC neurons were spontaneously active.
source: We found that the majority of MOC neurons had a resting membrane potential of −80.4 ± 0.8 mV (N = 56) and were silent at rest (only 3/59 neurons were spontaneously active), consistent with the low frequency of spontaneous activity observed in vivo (Fex, 1962; Cody and Johnstone, 1982; Robertson, 1984; Robertson and Gummer, 1985).

claim: The membrane capacitance (Cm) of MOC neurons was 36.5 ± 1.6 pF.
source: The membrane capacitance (Cm) and resistance (Rm) were 36.5 ± 1.6 pF and 123 ± 9 MΩ (N = 59), respectively.
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings.

claim: The membrane resistance (Rm) of MOC neurons was 123 ± 9 MΩ.
source: The membrane capacitance (Cm) and resistance (Rm) were 36.5 ± 1.6 pF and 123 ± 9 MΩ (N = 59), respectively.
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements from whole-cell patch-clamp recordings.

claim: MOC neurons lacked an apparent voltage 'sag' in response to hyperpolarizing current injections, indicating minimal expression of HCN channels.
source: In response to hyperpolarizing current injections, MOC neurons lacked an apparent voltage 'sag', indicating minimal expression of hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated (HCN) channels (Figure 2A).

claim: 57 out of 59 MOC neurons exhibited a biphasic after-hyperpolarization waveform following each spike.
source: Depolarizing currents near action potential threshold revealed a biphasic after-hyperpolarization waveform following each spike (Figure 2A, see arrowhead in +0.5 nA example, observed in 57/59 MOC neurons).

claim: MOC neurons fired action potentials that encoded stimulus current intensity with a remarkably linear increase in spike rate in response to increasing amplitude of 500-ms depolarizing current injections.
source: In response to the increasing amplitude of 500-ms depolarizing current injections, MOC neurons fired action potentials that encoded stimulus current intensity with a remarkably linear increase in spike rate (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Electrophysiological data showing linear input-output relationship.

claim: For injections up to 900 pA, MOC neurons responded with linearly increasing spike rates, with a slope of 0.150 Hz/pA.
source: For injections up to 900 pA, MOC neurons (N = 33) responded with linearly increasing spike rates, such that the rate nearly doubled when current injections were doubled in intensity, as reflected by the slope of a linear fit to the mean data (slope = 0.150 Hz/pA) (Figure 2C).

claim: The ratio of instantaneous spike rate during the last five action potentials compared to spikes #5–10 decreased with increasing current intensity.
source: The ratio of instantaneous spike rate during the last five action potentials (i.e., the steady-state frequency) compared to spikes #5–10 (initial frequency) decreased somewhat with increasing current intensity (Figure 2E & F); 0.86 ± 0.01 at 200 pA and 0.69 ± 0.02 at 900 pA (N = 11).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of spike rate adaptation.

claim: Individual MOC cells linearly encoded current intensity with both their initial and their steady-state instantaneous spike frequencies.
source: However, individual cells linearly encoded current intensity with both their initial and their steady-state instantaneous spike frequencies (initial slope = 0.255 Hz/pA; steady-state slope = 0.158 Hz/pA) (Figure 2F).

claim: Unilateral VCN injections with AAV1-CAG-ChR2-Venus-WPRE-SV40 resulted in Venus expression in VCN and Venus-positive fiber projections to the contralateral VNTB and rostral periolivary regions (RPO).
source: These injections resulted in Venus expression in VCN (Figure 3A) and Venus-positive fiber projections to the contralateral VNTB and rostral periolivary regions (RPO) (Figure 3B); moreover, Venus-positive boutons were observed in close proximity to MOC neuron dendrites and somata in the VNTB (Figure 3C).
evidence: Anatomical observation from viral tracing experiments.

claim: Venus-positive boutons were observed in close proximity to MOC neuron dendrites and somata in the VNTB.
source: These injections resulted in Venus expression in VCN (Figure 3A) and Venus-positive fiber projections to the contralateral VNTB and rostral periolivary regions (RPO) (Figure 3B); moreover, Venus-positive boutons were observed in close proximity to MOC neuron dendrites and somata in the VNTB (Figure 3C).
evidence: Anatomical observation from viral tracing experiments.

claim: Venus-positive VCN neurons reliably fired action potentials in response to repetitive 2 ms flashes of blue light.
source: Venus-positive VCN neurons reliably fired action potentials in response to repetitive 2 ms flashes of blue light (see example, Figure 3D).

claim: Reliable antidromic spiking of VCN neurons was observed when light flashes were delivered to axons outside the field of view of the recorded neuron.
source: Additionally, reliable antidromic spiking of VCN neurons was observed when light flashes were delivered to axons outside the field of view of the recorded neuron (N = 4).

claim: Light-evoked EPSCs in MOC neurons from VCN input were abolished with GYKI 53655, indicating they were glutamatergic and used AMPA receptors.
source: EPSCs were abolished with a selective non-competitive AMPA receptor antagonist, GYKI 53655 (50 µM, N = 3; not shown), indicating that they were glutamatergic and used AMPA receptors.

claim: The decay time constant of VCN-evoked EPSCs was best fit with either a single or double exponential equation.
source: For individual neurons held at −62.8 mV, 20 light-evoked EPSCs were averaged and their decay phases were best fit with either a single (N = 7) or double (N = 5) exponential equation.

claim: VCN inputs to MOC neurons exhibit inwardly rectifying current-voltage relations.
source: Current-voltage (I-V) relations were constructed by plotting the peak amplitude of EPSCs evoked at holding potentials between −82.8 and +57.2 mV (20 mV steps) and exhibited prominent inward rectification (Figure 3E–F).

claim: The voltage sensitivity of the peak currents and fast decay of the EPSCs from VCN input are strongly suggestive of postsynaptic GluA2-lacking Ca2+-permeable AMPARs.
source: The voltage sensitivity of the peak currents, together with the fast decay of the EPSCs, is strongly suggestive of postsynaptic GluA2-lacking Ca2+-permeable AMPARs (CP-AMPARs) (Mosbacher et al., 1994; Bowie and Mayer, 1995; Donevan and Rogawski, 1995; Geiger et al., 1995).
evidence: Inference based on electrophysiological properties and comparison to known receptor characteristics.

claim: T-stellate cells are the only VCN cell type that projects to the IC.
source: T-stellate (also called planar multipolar) cells of the VCN are excitatory projection neurons that receive auditory nerve inputs (Oertel et al., 2011). As a population, they may encode sound intensity and frequency spectrum. T-stellate cells are a major ascending pathway of the auditory system that projects widely to many targets and are the only VCN cell type that projects to the IC.
evidence: Statement based on established anatomical knowledge.

claim: An intersectional AAV approach was developed to selectively activate T-stellate cells.
source: We developed a scheme to selectively activate T-stellate cells using an intersectional AAV approach in order to perform virally driven optogenetic studies of ascending MOC circuitry (Figure 4Ai–ii).

claim: AAVrg-pmSyn1-EBFP-Cre injected into IC of ChAT-Cre/tdTomato mice caused Cre-dependent tdTomato expression in cells that project to and from IC, including T-stellate cells in the VCN.
source: An AAV engineered to infect axons in addition to neurons local to the injection site (AAVrg-pmSyn1-EBFP-Cre) (Tervo et al., 2016) was injected into IC of ChAT-Cre/tdTomato mice, causing Cre-dependent tdTomato expression in cells that project to and from IC, including T-stellate cells in the VCN (Figure 4Ai and Bii).
evidence: Anatomical observation from viral tracing experiments.

claim: Prior to AAV infection, no somata were positive for tdTomato in VCN or IC of ChAT-Cre/tdTomato mice.
source: Prior to AAV infection, no somata were positive for tdTomato in VCN or IC of ChAT-Cre/tdTomato mice (Figure 4Bi, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Anatomical observation confirming specificity of labeling.

claim: 1–2 weeks post IC infection with AAVrg-pmSyn1-EBFP-Cre, tdTomato-positive somata were located near the injection site and nuclei that send projections to IC.
source: 1–2 weeks post IC infection with AAVrg-pmSyn1-EBFP-Cre, tdTomato-positive somata were located near the injection site and nuclei that send projections to IC, including contralateral IC (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Anatomical observation from viral tracing experiments.

claim: A majority of retrogradely labeled VCN somata were located contralateral to the IC injection site.
source: A majority of retrogradely labeled VCN somata were located contralateral to the injection site (Figure 4Bii), whereas few were seen in ipsilateral VCN (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), reflecting previously described ipsilateral T-stellate cell projections (Adams, 1979; Thompson, 1998).
evidence: Anatomical observation from viral tracing experiments.

claim: All recordings from tdTomato-positive cells in VCN (N = 13) infected with AAVrg-pmSyn1-EBFP-Cre exhibited responses to current injections characteristic of T-stellate cells.
source: In recordings from tdTomato-positive VCN neurons (N = 15) in AAVrg-pmSyn1-EBFP-Cre-infected ChAT-Cre/tdTomato mice, all neurons exhibited responses to current injections that were characteristic of T-stellate cells (see example in Figure 4C).

claim: T-stellate cells fire action potentials tonically with a sustained rate in response to depolarizing current injections.
source: Action potentials fired tonically with a sustained rate in response to depolarizing current injections (Figure 4D).

claim: Hyperpolarizing current injections in T-stellate cells revealed a rectifying voltage response characteristic of HCN nonselective cation channels.
source: Hyperpolarizing current injections revealed a rectifying voltage response characteristic of HCN nonselective cation channels (Figure 4C).

claim: The membrane resistance (Rm) of T-stellate cells was 147.6 ± 21.5 MΩ.
source: Additionally, membrane resistance (Rm = 147.6 ± 21.5 MΩ) and membrane capacitance (Cm = 32.9 ± 2.6 pF) were typical of T-stellate cells (Wu and Oertel, 1987; Ferragamo et al., 1998; Golding et al., 1999).

claim: The membrane capacitance (Cm) of T-stellate cells was 32.9 ± 2.6 pF.
source: Additionally, membrane resistance (Rm = 147.6 ± 21.5 MΩ) and membrane capacitance (Cm = 32.9 ± 2.6 pF) were typical of T-stellate cells (Wu and Oertel, 1987; Ferragamo et al., 1998; Golding et al., 1999).

claim: VCN neurons positive for EYFP were also positive for tdTomato, confirming the selectivity of the intersectional AAV approach.
source: VCN neurons positive for EYFP were also positive for tdTomato (Figure 4Ei–F), confirming the selectivity of this intersectional AAV approach.
evidence: Anatomical observation confirming specificity of dual viral labeling.

claim: Dual infected VCN neurons projected to known T-stellate cell target nuclei, including contralateral IC, contralateral and ipsilateral VNTB, ipsilateral LSO, and contralateral lateral lemniscus.
source: Dual infected VCN neurons projected to known T-stellate cell target nuclei, including contralateral IC, contralateral and ipsilateral VNTB, ipsilateral LSO, and contralateral lateral lemniscus (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D-I).
evidence: Anatomical observation from viral tracing experiments.

claim: Optogenetic activation of T-stellate inputs evoked EPSCs in contralateral MOC neurons.
source: During whole-cell voltage-clamp recording, optogenetic activation of T-stellate inputs evoked EPSCs in contralateral MOC neurons (N = 4, Figure 4G), confirming that T-stellate neurons excite postsynaptic MOC efferent neurons.

claim: Decay kinetics of T-stellate inputs to MOC neurons were not significantly different compared to non-specific VCN inputs.
source: Decay kinetics of T-stellate inputs to MOC neurons were not significantly different compared to non-specific VCN inputs (Table 1), suggesting similar postsynaptic AMPA receptor compositions.

claim: At least a subset of IC-projecting T-stellate cells provide glutamatergic excitatory inputs to MOC neurons.
source: These results definitively show that at least a subset of IC-projecting T-stellate cells provide glutamatergic excitatory inputs to MOC neurons.
evidence: Conclusion based on optogenetic and electrophysiological data.

claim: Unilateral IC injections with AAV1-CAG-ChR2-Venus-WPRE-SV40 resulted in Venus expression in somata throughout the injected IC.
source: 1–2 weeks post-infection, Venus was observed in somata throughout the injected IC (Figure 5A).
evidence: Anatomical observation from viral tracing experiments.

claim: The majority of Venus-positive fibers from IC were visible in the ventral portion of the VNTB and RPO in close apposition to MOC neuron somata and dendrites.
source: The majority of Venus-positive fibers were visible in the ventral portion of the VNTB and RPO in close apposition to MOC neuron somata and dendrites (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Anatomical observation from viral tracing experiments.

claim: IC neurons positive for Venus fired action potentials in response to 2 ms flashes of blue light.
source: IC neurons positive for Venus fired action potentials in response to 2 ms flashes of blue light (see example in Figure 5C, N = 2), confirming that ChR2 currents could reliably elicit action potentials in response to high-frequency light stimuli.

claim: Evoked EPSCs originating from IC inputs were mediated by inwardly rectifying AMPARs.
source: Similar to VCN inputs onto MOC neurons, evoked EPSCs originating from IC inputs were mediated by inwardly rectifying AMPARs (Figure 5D–E).

claim: IC and VCN synapses onto MOC neurons both transmit by means of postsynaptic CP-AMPARs.
source: This suggests that IC and VCN synapses onto MOC neurons both transmit by means of postsynaptic CP-AMPARs.
evidence: Inference based on similar electrophysiological properties of EPSCs from both inputs.

claim: In the presence of intracellular spermine, glutamate-evoked currents in MOC neurons resulted in an inwardly rectifying I-V relation.
source: In the presence of intracellular spermine, glutamate-evoked currents resulted in an inwardly rectifying I-V relation (Figure 6A–B), similar to light-evoked EPSCs from IC or VCN input (Figure 3E–F and 5D–E).
evidence: Electrophysiological data from glutamate puff experiments.

claim: When recordings were made with a spermine-free solution, the I-V relation of glutamate-evoked currents in MOC neurons was linear.
source: When recordings were made with a spermine-free solution, the I-V relation was linear (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: Electrophysiological data from glutamate puff experiments.

claim: At +37.2 mV and +57.2 mV, 57.9% and 58.9% of the outward current was blocked by spermine, respectively.
source: At +37.2 mV and +57.2 mV, 57.9% and 58.9% of the outward current was blocked by spermine, respectively, suggesting that a majority of AMPAR-mediated currents are due to CP-AMPARs.

claim: After bath application of 25 µM IEM 1925, glutamate-evoked currents in MOC neurons were reduced by 55.3 ± 1.6%.
source: After bath application of 25 µM IEM 1925, glutamate-evoked currents were reduced by 55.3 ± 1.6% and returned to 81.2 ± 3.0% of control after wash (N = 3, Figure 6C).

claim: The percentage of block by IEM 1925 was similar to that of spermine block in dialysis experiments.
source: This percentage of block by IEM 1925 was similar to that of spermine block in our dialysis experiments (Figure 6B).
evidence: Comparison of pharmacological and dialysis data.

claim: The blocking effect of IEM 1925 on glutamate-evoked currents pharmacologically confirmed that MOC neurons express GluA2-lacking CP-AMPARs.
source: The blocking effect of IEM 1925 on glutamate-evoked currents pharmacologically confirmed that MOC neurons express GluA2-lacking CP-AMPARs.

claim: The decay phase of average miniature events in MOC neurons was best fit with a double exponential function, where τfast was responsible for 89.0 ± 3.0% of the mEPSC amplitude.
source: The decay phase of average miniature events was best fit with a double exponential function, where τfast was responsible for 89.0 ± 3.0% of the mEPSC amplitude (see Table 1 and example in Figure 6D).

claim: The average τfast and τslow of mEPSCs in MOC neurons were 0.17 ± 0.01 ms and 1.72 ± 0.43 ms, respectively.
source: The average τfast and τslow of mEPSCs were 0.17 ± 0.01 ms and 1.72 ± 0.43 ms, respectively (N = 3 neurons, 1873 mEPSCs).

claim: The distribution of binned mEPSC inter-event intervals was best described with a single exponential equation (τ = 0.20 s), reflecting that the miniature events were stochastic in nature.
source: The distribution of binned mEPSC IEIs was best described with a single exponential equation (τ = 0.20 s), reflecting that the miniature events were stochastic in nature (Fatt and Katz, 1952).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of mEPSC timing and comparison to known stochastic release properties.

claim: The average and median mEPSC amplitudes in MOC neurons were 57.5 ± 0.9 pA and 52.5 pA, respectively.
source: The average and median mEPSC amplitudes were 57.5 ± 0.9 pA and 52.5 pA, respectively, and ranged from 27.2 pA to 146.9 pA (Figure 6F).

claim: The majority of mEPSCs in MOC neurons were due to fast-gating AMPARs.
source: In comparison with light-evoked EPSCs from IC and VCN (Table 1), these results confirmed that the majority of mEPSCs were due to fast-gating AMPARs.
evidence: Comparison of mEPSC kinetics to evoked EPSC kinetics.

claim: Fast-gating CP-AMPARs are the major component of excitatory synaptic transmission at MOC neurons.
source: Together, supportive of data from light-evoked EPSCs and glutamate-puff-evoked currents, these results suggest that fast-gating CP-AMPARs are the major component of excitatory synaptic transmission at MOC neurons.
evidence: Synthesis of multiple lines of evidence.

claim: During 20-pulse tetanus stimuli (20 or 50 Hz), light-evoked VCN-originating EPSCs depressed whereas IC-originating EPSCs facilitated.
source: During 20-pulse tetanus stimuli (20 or 50 Hz), light-evoked VCN-originating EPSCs depressed whereas IC-originating EPSCs facilitated (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: Electrophysiological data from repetitive stimulation experiments.

claim: VCN inputs showed about 70% depression, with no difference between 20 Hz or 50 Hz activity.
source: This 'plasticity index' showed about 70% depression for VCN inputs, with no difference between 20 Hz or 50 Hz activity (0.31 ± 0.02 for 20 Hz, N = 8; 0.29 ± 0.04 for 50 Hz, N = 7; p = 0.59, Student's t-test; Figure 7C).

claim: Inputs from IC showed marked enhancement of the plasticity index during the train, with no differences between 20 Hz and 50 Hz.
source: By contrast, inputs from IC showed marked enhancement of the plasticity index during the train, although again with no differences between 20 Hz and 50 Hz (1.82 ± 0.17 for 20 Hz, N = 8; 1.65 ± 0.26 for 50 Hz N = 7; p = 0.59, Student's t-test; Figure 7C).

claim: The degree of plasticity was independent of whether ChR2 was excited near or far from synaptic terminals.
source: The degree of plasticity was independent of whether ChR2 was excited near or far from synaptic terminals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Control experiment ruling out artifact from optogenetic stimulation.

claim: Depression observed by VCN input recovered with a time course (τ20 Hz = 3.5 ± 0.7 s, τ50 Hz = 3.1 ± 0.4 s) comparable to the recovery from IC input facilitation (τ20 Hz = 4.5 ± 1.4 s, τ50 Hz = 4.4 ± 1.7 s).
source: We fit recovery data with single exponential functions and found that depression observed by VCN input recovered with a time course (τ20 Hz = 3.5 ± 0.7 s, τ50 Hz = 3.1 ± 0.4 s) comparable to the recovery from IC input facilitation (τ20 Hz = 4.5 ± 1.4 s, τ50 Hz = 4.4 ± 1.7 s; Figure 7E).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of recovery from short-term plasticity.

claim: IC input facilitation onto MOC neurons lasted for tens of seconds, resembling synaptic augmentation.
source: While classical short-term facilitation lasts for only hundreds of milliseconds after tetanus stimuli (Zucker and Regehr, 2002), IC input facilitation onto MOC neurons lasted for tens of seconds. This longer lasting facilitation resembles synaptic augmentation, which has a longer lifespan (seconds) than classical short-term facilitation (milliseconds) and a recovery time course that is insensitive to the duration or frequency of repetitive activation (Magleby, 1987; Zucker and Regehr, 2002).
evidence: Comparison of observed plasticity to known forms of synaptic plasticity.

claim: Each MOC neuron in the brain slice receives an average of 4.2 ± 1.0 unilateral inputs from the IC (maximum of 13.8).
source: However, comparing average minimally stimulated light responses to maximal light responses from our in vitro data, we estimated that each MOC neuron in the brain slice receives an average of 4.2 ± 1.0 unilateral inputs from the IC (maximum of 13.8, N = 15) and 11.1 ± 2.4 unilateral inputs from the VCN (maximum of 35.5, N = 15).

claim: Each MOC neuron in the brain slice receives an average of 11.1 ± 2.4 unilateral inputs from the VCN (maximum of 35.5).
source: However, comparing average minimally stimulated light responses to maximal light responses from our in vitro data, we estimated that each MOC neuron in the brain slice receives an average of 4.2 ± 1.0 unilateral inputs from the IC (maximum of 13.8, N = 15) and 11.1 ± 2.4 unilateral inputs from the VCN (maximum of 35.5, N = 15).

claim: Unitary responses from IC inputs were measured to have a maximum conductance (Gmax) of 0.40 ± 0.01 nS.
source: Unitary responses were measured to have a maximum conductance (Gmax) of 0.40 ± 0.01 nS for IC inputs (N = 3) and 0.46 ± 0.06 nS for VCN inputs (N = 3).
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements from minimal stimulation experiments.

claim: Unitary responses from VCN inputs were measured to have a maximum conductance (Gmax) of 0.46 ± 0.06 nS.
source: Unitary responses were measured to have a maximum conductance (Gmax) of 0.40 ± 0.01 nS for IC inputs (N = 3) and 0.46 ± 0.06 nS for VCN inputs (N = 3).
evidence: Electrophysiological measurements from minimal stimulation experiments.

claim: In response to a small number of facilitating inputs (10 or 20) firing at ~40 Hz, few action potentials were evoked in MOC neurons.
source: In response to a small number of facilitating inputs (labeled 'Fac' in the following figures) firing at ~40 Hz, few action potentials were evoked in MOC neurons (1.8 ± 0.8 for 10 inputs and 5.3 ± 1.5 for 20 inputs, N = 6) (Figure 8Bi, D, and E), and the first peak of postsynaptic firing generally occurred hundreds of milliseconds after stimulus onset (271.1 ± 74.4 ms for 10 inputs and 183.8 ± 59.0 ms for 20 inputs, N = 6) (Figure 8Bi, D, and F).

claim: With only 10 facilitating inputs at ~40 Hz, two out of six MOC neurons failed to reach action potential threshold.
source: With only 10 facilitating inputs at ~40 Hz, two out of six MOC neurons failed to reach action potential threshold (e.g., first row of Figure 9C).

claim: MOC neurons responded to increasing numbers of facilitating inputs, with a linearly increasing number of spikes during each stimulus for both ~40 Hz and ~180 Hz paradigms.
source: MOC neurons responded to increasing numbers of facilitating inputs, with a linearly increasing number of spikes during each stimulus for both ~40 Hz and ~180 Hz paradigms (Figure 8E).

claim: Facilitating EPSGs at ~180 Hz generally elicited more action potentials with an earlier onset than ~40 Hz EPSGs with the same number of inputs.
source: Facilitating EPSGs at ~180 Hz generally elicited more action potentials with an earlier onset than ~40 Hz EPSGs with the same number of inputs (Figure 8Bii,E, and F).

claim: The firing sensitivity (FS) of MOC neurons to facilitating inputs was 0.31 ± 0.06 for 40 Hz and 1.0 ± 0.1 for 183 Hz.
source: FS was 0.31 ± 0.06 for 40 Hz and 1.0 ± 0.1 for 183 Hz (p = 6.7 × 10−6; paired samples Student's t-test).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of conductance-clamp simulation data.

claim: Some MOC neurons failed to reach action potential threshold in response to depressing waveforms at ~40 Hz (6/6 failures with 10 inputs and 3/6 with 20 inputs) and ~180 Hz (3/6 failures with 10 inputs).
source: Some MOC neurons failed to reach action potential threshold in response to depressing waveforms at ~40 Hz (6/6 failures with 10 inputs and 3/6 with 20 inputs) and ~180 Hz (3/6 failures with 10 inputs) (e.g., last two rows of Figure 8D).

claim: The firing sensitivity (FS) of MOC neurons to depressing inputs was 0.095 ± 0.014 for 40 Hz and 0.31 ± 0.08 for 180 Hz.
source: FS was 0.095 ± 0.014 for 40 Hz and 0.31 ± 0.08 for 180 Hz (p = 1.6 × 10−4, paired samples Student's t-test).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of conductance-clamp simulation data.

claim: When action potentials were elicited and the number of simulated inputs were equivalent, depressing waveforms at ~180 Hz always drove MOC neurons to threshold earlier than those at ~40 Hz.
source: When action potentials were elicited and the number of simulated inputs were equivalent, depressing waveforms at ~180 Hz always drove MOC neurons to threshold earlier than those at ~40 Hz (Figure 8F).

claim: Simulated VCN-like (depressing) EPSGs could only drive the firing rate to about half of the maximum rates measured in vivo (47.8 ± 5.9 Hz average maximum).
source: As our previously described experiments demonstrated that inputs from IC facilitated and those from VCN depressed (Figure 7), our simulated inputs suggest that, individually, VCN inputs best drive slow rates of sustained activity in MOC neurons and IC inputs best drive high rates of activity. Combinations of these inputs are needed to access the full dynamic range of MOC neuron firing, as our simulated VCN-like (depressing) EPSGs could only drive the firing rate (47.8 ± 5.9 Hz average maximum, N = 6) to about half of the maximum rates measured in vivo (Liberman, 1988; Brown, 1989), while IC-like (facilitating) EPSGs could drive MOC neurons to fire at maximal rates (180 ± 12 Hz average maximum, N = 6) more comparable to our in vitro experiments (Figure 2).
evidence: Conductance-clamp simulation data and comparison to in vivo data.

claim: IC-like (facilitating) EPSGs could drive MOC neurons to fire at maximal rates (180 ± 12 Hz average maximum) more comparable to in vitro experiments.
source: As our previously described experiments demonstrated that inputs from IC facilitated and those from VCN depressed (Figure 7), our simulated inputs suggest that, individually, VCN inputs best drive slow rates of sustained activity in MOC neurons and IC inputs best drive high rates of activity. Combinations of these inputs are needed to access the full dynamic range of MOC neuron firing, as our simulated VCN-like (depressing) EPSGs could only drive the firing rate (47.8 ± 5.9 Hz average maximum, N = 6) to about half of the maximum rates measured in vivo (Liberman, 1988; Brown, 1989), while IC-like (facilitating) EPSGs could drive MOC neurons to fire at maximal rates (180 ± 12 Hz average maximum, N = 6) more comparable to our in vitro experiments (Figure 2).
evidence: Conductance-clamp simulation data and comparison to in vitro data.

claim: Using the ~180 Hz paradigm, 20 depressing inputs elicited a low number of action potentials in MOC neurons without any failures (5.5 ± 1.4 spikes on average).
source: Using the ~180 Hz paradigm, 20 depressing inputs elicited a low number of action potentials in MOC neurons without any failures (5.5 ± 1.4 spikes on average, N = 6) (dashed gray line, Figure 9D), with the first action potential occurring at 36.5 ± 6.6 ms after the stimuli onset (dashed gray line, Figure 9E).

claim: The number of action potentials evoked by facilitating or depressing input was increased when both types were combined.
source: As expected, the number of action potentials evoked by facilitating or depressing input was increased when the both types were combined (Figure 9B–D).

claim: Spikes evoked by weaker facilitating inputs (10 inputs at ~40 Hz and ~110 Hz) were significantly enhanced when combined with the depressing paradigm.
source: However, the magnitude of this effect was dependent on the strength of the facilitating input, as spikes evoked by weaker facilitating inputs (1.6 ± 0.8 spikes on average for 10 inputs at ~40 Hz and 8.6 ± 2.6 spikes at ~110 Hz) were significantly enhanced when combined with the depressing paradigm (9.2 ± 2.3 spikes at ~40 Hz, 16.1 ± 3.1 spikes at ~110 Hz) (p = 0.022 at ~40 Hz and p = 0.0034 at ~110 Hz; paired samples Student's t-test), whereas stronger facilitating inputs were not enhanced (for example, 67.3 ± 8.0 spikes on average for 80 inputs at ~110 Hz vs 68.7 ± 0.4 when combined) (Figure 9D).
evidence: Conductance-clamp simulation data with statistical analysis.

claim: Stronger facilitating inputs were not enhanced when combined with depressing inputs.
source: However, the magnitude of this effect was dependent on the strength of the facilitating input, as spikes evoked by weaker facilitating inputs (1.6 ± 0.8 spikes on average for 10 inputs at ~40 Hz and 8.6 ± 2.6 spikes at ~110 Hz) were significantly enhanced when combined with the depressing paradigm (9.2 ± 2.3 spikes at ~40 Hz, 16.1 ± 3.1 spikes at ~110 Hz) (p = 0.022 at ~40 Hz and p = 0.0034 at ~110 Hz; paired samples Student's t-test), whereas stronger facilitating inputs were not enhanced (for example, 67.3 ± 8.0 spikes on average for 80 inputs at ~110 Hz vs 68.7 ± 0.4 when combined) (Figure 9D).
evidence: Conductance-clamp simulation data with statistical analysis.

claim: The firing sensitivity (FS) of facilitating inputs (0.32 ± 0.06 at ~40 Hz and 0.82 ± 0.18 at ~110 Hz) was not significantly altered with the addition of a depressing input (0.30 ± 0.09 at ~40 Hz and 0.74 ± 0.12 at ~110 Hz).
source: The FS of facilitating inputs (0.32 ± 0.06 at ~40 Hz and 0.82 ± 0.18 at ~110 Hz) was not significantly altered with the addition of a depressing input (0.30 ± 0.09 at ~40 Hz and 0.74 ± 0.12 at ~110 Hz, N = 5) (p = 0.38 at ~40 Hz and p = 0.088 at ~110 Hz; paired samples Student's t-test) (Figure 9D), demonstrating that MOC neurons generally summate concurrent inputs and confirming that they linearly respond to signals in proportion to the intensity of their input (Figure 2).
evidence: Conductance-clamp simulation data with statistical analysis.

claim: Relatively weak descending inputs to MOC neurons are enhanced when combined with the ascending input.
source: Overall, these results suggest that relatively weak descending inputs to MOC neurons are enhanced when combined with the ascending input, while relatively strong descending inputs override the ascending input—evoking an equivalent amount of spikes with similar onset, whether or not the ascending input is active.

claim: Relatively strong descending inputs override the ascending input, evoking an equivalent amount of spikes with similar onset, whether or not the ascending input is active.
source: Overall, these results suggest that relatively weak descending inputs to MOC neurons are enhanced when combined with the ascending input, while relatively strong descending inputs override the ascending input—evoking an equivalent amount of spikes with similar onset, whether or not the ascending input is active.

claim: The data confirm the potency of the descending control of the MOC system, as compared to the reflex pathway.
source: The data, therefore, confirm the potency of the descending control of the MOC system, as compared to the reflex pathway.
evidence: Conclusion based on conductance-clamp simulation data.

claim: The MOC system may serve to protect the cochlea from acoustic trauma.
source: The medial olivocochlear (MOC) system provides many of these efferent fibers, and may serve to protect the cochlea from acoustic trauma (Rajan, 1988; Kujawa and Liberman, 1997; Darrow et al., 2007) and to dynamically enhance the detection of salient sound in diverse sensory environments (Winslow and Sachs, 1987; Kawase and Liberman, 1993) by controlling cochlear gain in a frequency- and intensity-specific manner.

claim: The MOC system may dynamically enhance the detection of salient sound in diverse sensory environments by controlling cochlear gain in a frequency- and intensity-specific manner.
source: The medial olivocochlear (MOC) system provides many of these efferent fibers, and may serve to protect the cochlea from acoustic trauma (Rajan, 1988; Kujawa and Liberman, 1997; Darrow et al., 2007) and to dynamically enhance the detection of salient sound in diverse sensory environments (Winslow and Sachs, 1987; Kawase and Liberman, 1993) by controlling cochlear gain in a frequency- and intensity-specific manner.

claim: MOC efferent fibers arise from cholinergic neurons whose somata primarily reside in the ventral nucleus of the trapezoid body (VNTB) of the superior olivary complex (SOC).
source: MOC efferent fibers arise from cholinergic neurons whose somata primarily reside in the ventral nucleus of the trapezoid body (VNTB) of the superior olivary complex (SOC) (Warr, 1975) and project to outer hair cells in the cochlea (Guinan et al., 1983; Guinan et al., 1984; Wilson et al., 1991), and this peripheral control by efferents has been extensively studied (Guinan, 2010; Guinan, 2018).

claim: MOC efferent fibers project to outer hair cells in the cochlea.
source: MOC efferent fibers arise from cholinergic neurons whose somata primarily reside in the ventral nucleus of the trapezoid body (VNTB) of the superior olivary complex (SOC) (Warr, 1975) and project to outer hair cells in the cochlea (Guinan et al., 1983; Guinan et al., 1984; Wilson et al., 1991), and this peripheral control by efferents has been extensively studied (Guinan, 2010; Guinan, 2018).

claim: MOC fibers respond to sound and form a negative feedback system, described as a reflex providing frequency-specific feedback to the cochlea.
source: MOC fibers respond to sound and form a negative feedback system, and is thus described as a reflex providing frequency-specific feedback to the cochlea (Liberman and Brown, 1986; Winslow and Sachs, 1987; Brown, 2016).

claim: This feedback is mediated by acetylcholine released from terminals of MOC fibers, thereby inhibiting outer hair cell motility and decreasing cochlear sensitivity.
source: This feedback is mediated by acetylcholine released from terminals of MOC fibers, thereby inhibiting outer hair cell motility and decreasing cochlear sensitivity (Wiederhold and Kiang, 1970).

claim: Excitatory synaptic inputs that modulate and control MOC neuron function are made both by ascending inputs from the cochlear nucleus and by descending inputs from areas that include brainstem, inferior colliculus (IC), and auditory cortex.
source: For example, excitatory synaptic inputs that modulate and control MOC neuron function are made both by ascending inputs from the cochlear nucleus (termed here the 'reflex pathway') and by descending inputs from areas that include brainstem, inferior colliculus (IC), and auditory cortex (Thompson and Thompson, 1993; Vetter et al., 1993; Mulders and Robertson, 2002).

claim: The reflex MOC pathway receives ascending auditory inputs from principal neurons in the ventral cochlear nucleus (VCN), possibly by T-stellate cells.
source: The reflex MOC pathway receives ascending auditory inputs from principal neurons in the ventral cochlear nucleus (VCN), possibly by T-stellate cells (Thompson and Thompson, 1991; de Venecia et al., 2005; Darrow et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2013).

claim: T-stellate cells are anatomically and physiologically well suited to provide auditory information to MOC neurons.
source: While T-stellate cells are anatomically and physiologically well suited to provide auditory information to MOC neurons (Oertel et al., 2011) and receive inputs from type I spiral ganglion neurons, whose axons form the auditory nerve, in fact no direct evidence shows that these neurons activate MOC neurons.
evidence: Statement based on cited literature and inference.

claim: Descending projections from the IC contact MOC neurons.
source: Descending projections from the IC contact MOC neurons (Faye-Lund, 1986; Thompson and Thompson, 1993; Vetter et al., 1993) and are tonotopically arranged, as low-frequency fibers project laterally and high frequencies increasingly project more medially (Caicedo and Herbert, 1993; Suthakar and Ryugo, 2017).

claim: Descending projections from the IC to MOC neurons are tonotopically arranged, as low-frequency fibers project laterally and high frequencies increasingly project more medially.
source: Descending projections from the IC contact MOC neurons (Faye-Lund, 1986; Thompson and Thompson, 1993; Vetter et al., 1993) and are tonotopically arranged, as low-frequency fibers project laterally and high frequencies increasingly project more medially (Caicedo and Herbert, 1993; Suthakar and Ryugo, 2017).

claim: Descending inputs may utilize the MOC system to suppress cochlear inputs during non-auditory tasks.
source: Descending inputs may utilize the MOC system to suppress cochlear inputs during non-auditory tasks (Delano et al., 2007; Wittekindt et al., 2014) and are well positioned to aid sound detection in noise by contextually inhibiting background frequency spectra (Farhadi et al., 2021).

claim: Descending inputs are well positioned to aid sound detection in noise by contextually inhibiting background frequency spectra.
source: Descending inputs may utilize the MOC system to suppress cochlear inputs during non-auditory tasks (Delano et al., 2007; Wittekindt et al., 2014) and are well positioned to aid sound detection in noise by contextually inhibiting background frequency spectra (Farhadi et al., 2021).

claim: Combinations of facilitating and depressing inputs enabled firing of MOC neurons over a surprisingly wide dynamic range.
source: By using a conductance-clamp approach, we found that combinations of facilitating and depressing inputs enabled firing of MOC neurons over a surprisingly wide dynamic range, suggesting an essential role for descending signaling to a brainstem nucleus.
evidence: Conclusion based on conductance-clamp simulation data.

claim: The results suggest an essential role for descending signaling to a brainstem nucleus.
